summary: Defines how NETCONF, the protocol for configuring network devices, can deliver asynchronous notifications. An optional capability built on the base protocol, it specifies the operations and capabilities needed so a client can subscribe and be told about events on a device as they happen, rather than polling.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking your oven every minute whether the cake is done, you ask it to ring a bell. This lets a network device ring a bell when something happens.

questions: how to subscribe to netconf events
what is the netconf event stream
subtitle: How a NETCONF client subscribes to a device and gets events pushed to it as they happen.

tldr.problem: NETCONF is a request and reply protocol, so a manager that wants to know about faults or changes on a device has no way to be told asynchronously.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a create-subscription operation, optionally naming an event stream, a filter and a replay time range. The server then sends one-way notification messages over the same session as events occur.
tldr.outcome: It is an optional capability, advertised during the capability exchange, that uses the same XML data model and security model as the rest of NETCONF.

today: RFC 5277 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why NETCONF Needs Notifications
sections.content:
RFC 5277 defines an asynchronous message delivery service for NETCONF, the network configuration protocol. It is an optional capability built on top of the base NETCONF definition, and the RFC defines the capabilities and operations needed to support it.

The motivation is to send asynchronous messages that fit the same data model and security model that a NETCONF implementation already uses. Notifications should be carried over a connection-oriented mechanism, be understandable without protocol information, support filtering in the server, and allow the server to replay locally logged notifications.

A NETCONF server does not send notifications before it is asked. The client starts the flow by creating a subscription, and the subscription cannot be modified once it has been created.
sections.eli5: Normally the manager has to keep asking the device what is going on. This RFC lets the manager say once, tell me when something happens, and then wait.

sections.title: Creating a Subscription and Receiving Notifications
sections.content:
The client sends <create-subscription>. It has four optional parameters: <stream> picks the event stream (the default NETCONF stream if absent), <filter> selects a subset of events, and <startTime> and <stopTime> select a time range for replay. If the server can satisfy the request it answers with <ok>. Otherwise it returns an <rpc-error>, for example for an invalid filter, a non-existent stream, or a <stopTime> given without a <startTime>.

After that the server sends <notification> messages whenever an event of interest occurs. A notification is a complete, well-formed XML document and is a one-way message, not an RPC, so there is no response. Its only required content is <eventTime>, the time the event was generated by the event source; the rest of the content is outside this document.

The subscription ends when the session is closed with <close-session>, when the session or its transport is terminated (for example with <kill-session> from another session), or after the stop time if one was given. In the stop time case the NETCONF session stays active.
sections.eli5: You hand the device a note saying which bells you want to hear. It answers okay, and from then on it rings the bell each time one of those things happens. You do not have to answer the bell.

sections.title: Event Streams and Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
Support is advertised in the capability exchange with the identifier urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:notification:1.0. An event stream is a set of event notifications matching some forwarding criteria. Streams are predefined on the device, and their configuration is outside the scope of the RFC. A notification can belong to more than one stream, and a subscription is bound to a single stream for its lifetime.

A server that supports notifications MUST support the stream named exactly NETCONF. The contents of all streams MUST be encoded in XML. Other sources such as SNMP or syslog are allowed but not specified.

A client discovers streams with a <get> on the <streams> subtree. Each stream has a mandatory unique <name>, a <description> and a <replaySupport> flag. The server applies access control after building each notification, and a session without permission to receive it simply does not get it.
sections.eli5: A stream is like a radio channel. The device has a few channels, one called NETCONF that every device must have, and you pick which one to listen to.

sections.title: Replaying Logged Notifications
sections.content:
If a stream keeps a log, a client can ask for old notifications by giving <startTime> in <create-subscription>. A start time later than the current time is an error. If it is earlier than the log reaches, replay begins with the earliest available notification. Times are matched against when the event was generated, and implementations must support time zones.

The server cannot be expected to keep an unlimited log. Clients can read <replayLogCreationTime> and <replayLogAgedTime> to see what is available. How many notifications are stored is up to the server.

When replay is finished the server sends a <replayComplete> notification, which cannot be filtered out and is sent for no other reason. If a <stopTime> was given, a <notificationComplete> notification follows and the session becomes an ordinary command and response session again. Without a stop time, notifications generated since the subscription was created are sent next, followed by new ones as they arise.
sections.eli5: Replay is like asking the device to read you the messages you missed while you were out, then saying that is all of the old ones, and carrying on with the new ones.

sections.title: Filtering Notifications
sections.content:
A filter is given only when the subscription is created and exists only as a parameter of that subscription. It does not change the stream configuration. It is applied to the content inside the <notification> wrapper, not to the wrapper itself. Either subtree or XPath filtering can be used, and XPath works for notifications only if the server advertises the XPath capability.

If a filter looks for a value that the notification does not contain, the notification is filtered out. For subtree filtering, a non-empty node set means a match.

The RFC notes that subtree filtering supports only equality comparisons and logical OR, so it suits simple filters, such as selecting fault events with severity critical, major or minor. XPath can express the same selection in a single expression. The examples use a fictional event schema made up for the RFC.
sections.eli5: A filter is a list of what you care about. If you only want to hear about big problems, the device keeps quiet about small ones.

sections.title: The Interleave Capability
sections.content:
While a subscription is active, a server MUST accept and process <close-session>. It MAY accept other operations, and otherwise it rejects them with a resource-denied error.

A server that does accept other operations on a subscribed session advertises the :interleave capability, identified by urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:interleave:1.0. This lets one session carry both notifications and normal requests, which reduces the number of sessions an operator or management application needs. The capability depends on the notification capability and defines no new operations. Sending a second <create-subscription> on a session that already has an active subscription returns an operation-failed error.
sections.eli5: Without this, a session listening for bells cannot do anything else. With it, you can listen and still ask questions on the same line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of base NETCONF also apply. Notifications are never sent before the transport and NETCONF layers, including the capability exchange, are established and the manager is identified and authenticated.

A <create-subscription> can be seen as a deferred <get>, so what a user can receive depends on what that user is allowed to see. The server MUST NOT include any content in a notification that the user is not authorized to view. Stream names and notification content can be sensitive. Carrying syslog or SNMP data over NETCONF may make it more or less vulnerable than its usual transport.

A malicious or buggy client that sends many subscriptions can use up system resources. Such subscriptions can be ended by terminating the underlying sessions with <kill-session>. If a subscription had a stop time, the client is responsible for closing the session afterwards.
sections.eli5: The device only rings a bell for people who are allowed to hear it, and it never tells anyone secrets they are not cleared to know.
